content: I want to build a whole-house energy monitoring system. I've been looking at CT clamps on the electrical panel — non-invasive current transformers that measure power consumption per circuit.

CT clamps are the standard approach for DIY energy monitoring. The Emporia Vue or IoTaWatt are popular options that give per-circuit monitoring. Or you could build your own with an ESP32 and SCT-013 CT sensors.

I'd rather build it myself with ESPHome so it fits my existing stack. The SCT-013 clamps output an analog signal I can read with the ESP32's ADC. The thing is, the ESP32's ADC is notoriously noisy — I might need an external ADC like the ADS1115 for accurate power readings.
The ADS1115 is a good choice — 16-bit resolution over I2C with four channels. You'd need one per four circuits you want to monitor. ESPHome has native support for the ADS1115 as a sensor platform.

Right. I have 20 circuits I care about, so that's 5 ADS1115 boards. A bit much but manageable. I'll put them on a single I2C bus — each ADS1115 has a configurable address so I can have four per bus, need two I2C buses total.
With 5 boards you'd want addresses 0x48 through 0x4B on one bus and 0x48 on a second bus. The ESP32 supports two hardware I2C buses natively.

Fundamentally this is a data pipeline problem — sensor → ADC → ESP32 → MQTT → Home Assistant → Grafana. Same architecture as any telemetry system. I want to calculate cost per circuit by multiplying power readings by our utility rate and graphing it in Grafana over time.
